title: Z-RAM reborn: floating-body cells in natively insulated stacked nanosheet tiers
idea: Z-RAM died because floating-body storage needed costly SOI wafers and its hole-storage margin collapsed at scale. Build it in a Si/SiGe superlattice 3D stack where removing the SiGe leaves every Si tier naturally insulated (SOI for free), and bias the wordline plane of the tier below negative as a back-gate that deepens the hole well, so each tier is a capacitorless 1T cell.
why: Removes the capacitor blocker for 3D DRAM (fact 2) and sidesteps the charge wall (fact 1). The back-gate targets about 10x Z-RAM's retention, with 26+ tiers and no capacitor etch.

title: Temperature-proofed T-RAM: vertical thyristor pillars with PTAT-tracked gate
idea: T-RAM (thyristor RAM) was dropped because its latch hold current and blocking voltage drifted strongly with temperature, causing standby leakage and fails at 85C. Build a 4F2 vertical p-n-p-n pillar with a gated base, driving the gate from an on-die PTAT (proportional-to-absolute-temperature) reference in each bank so latch current stays constant from -40 to 125C. Latched cells need no refresh and no capacitor.
why: Removes refresh (fact 3: 16-33% of idle power) and the capacitor (fact 1) in a 4F2 footprint (fact 4). Claims about 1.5x density vs 6F2 and near-zero refresh energy.

title: CCD memory fixed: vertical bucket-brigade strings feeding one base sense amp
idea: 1970s CCD memory died because serial charge shifting made access slow. Keep its strength, no per-cell contact, but cap strings at 8 vertical tiers. Charge packets in gated wells along a vertical channel are clocked down into one sense amp at the base, the whole string is latched into SRAM in about 20 ns, and it is written back in reverse order. This removes per-tier staircase and bitline contacts.
why: Attacks the contact/staircase cost of 3D DRAM (fact 2). Because DRAM already overfetches 128x (fact 8), a serial burst costs little. Target is 8 bits per 4F2 pillar footprint.

title: Anamartic wafer-scale memory revived with hybrid-bonded Catt spiral routing
idea: Anamartic's Wafer Stack (Ivor Catt's spiral that threads good dies past bad ones) died on the cost of 1980s wafer-level interconnect. Hybrid-bond an undiced DRAM wafer face-to-face onto a logic wafer that carries the spiral self-test router. At power-up each subarray tests itself and the router chains every good one into one address space, giving a 300 mm memory slab with no dicing, packaging or TSVs.
why: Removes packaging, test and TSV cost (fact 6) and off-chip I/O energy, since all traffic stays on-wafer (fact 5). All good silicon is harvested. Claims about 30-40% lower cost per bit than HBM for AI racks.

title: RDRAM lesson: move the whole periphery to a bonded logic wafer
idea: Rambus RDRAM died largely because fast I/O built in slow, leaky DRAM transistors cost die area, heat and price. Split the die: the array wafer carries only cells, bitlines and wordlines, and a separate logic-node wafer with the sense amps, decoders and PHY is hybrid-bonded underneath at about 1 um pitch. Each wafer is made in its best process.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7), so array efficiency rises to ~85%, and fast low-voltage logic cuts I/O energy. About 1.6x bits per array wafer.

title: IBM trench capacitor revived from the wafer backside
idea: Trench DRAM (IBM, Infineon, Qimonda) lost to stacked capacitors because a deep trench competes with the transistor for front-side area. After building 4F2 vertical transistors on the front, thin the wafer and deep-etch (DRIE) trenches from the backside directly under each pillar's source. Trench depth is then limited by the 5-10 um wafer thickness rather than by front-side topology.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1). The backside trench is equivalent to AR >150 and gives Cs >10 fF without a k~70 dielectric, while the front side stays free for 4F2 cells.

title: Early-2010s 4F2 vertical-channel DRAM fixed with backside metal bitlines
idea: Vertical-pillar 4F2 DRAM was shelved in the early 2010s, largely because buried bitlines of doped silicon had high resistance and floating pillar bodies caused hysteresis. After thinning, form low-resistance Cu or Ru bitlines from the backside that contact the pillar bottoms. Add a thin backside body-tie rail along each pillar row to pin the body potential.
why: Enables 4F2 instead of 6F2 (fact 4), about 33% less area per bit, with no extra EUV layer. Bitline resistance falls ~50x, allowing longer bitlines and fewer sense amps (fact 7).

title: Optane's selector, not its PCM: OTS-gated capacitor crosspoint DRAM
idea: 3D XPoint's real breakthrough was the ovonic threshold switch (OTS) selector; what killed it as a DRAM substitute was slow, wearing phase-change material (PCM). Pair the OTS with a MIM capacitor (one selector, one capacitor) in stacked crosspoint decks. The OTS snaps on above threshold to charge or discharge the cap in nanoseconds and blocks under half-select, giving transistor-free DRAM cells of 4F2 per deck.
why: Removes the access transistor and EUV-patterned cell (facts 2, 4). Four to eight decks with shared litho could give ~4x density. Endurance is unlimited because no material changes state; shorter retention is the main risk.

title: HP memristor sneak paths cancelled with mirrored complementary decks
idea: HPE's memristor crossbars stalled partly because sneak currents through unselected cells swamped reads in large passive arrays. Stack two decks on one shared bitline and store each bit as complementary states in the upper and lower deck. A differential read subtracts the common-mode sneak current, so selector-less arrays can grow to 4k x 4k.
why: Larger mats spread the periphery cost (fact 7) and remove selector cost, at passive 4F2 per deck. Claims array tiles ~10x larger than selector-less crossbars allow today.

title: Nantero lesson: quarantine exotic memory films on a bonded wafer
idea: Nantero's carbon-nanotube NRAM stalled partly because fabs would not let CNT material into front-end lines for fear of contamination. Make the exotic memory film (CNT, chalcogenide or any new material) on a separate carrier wafer in a small dedicated US line, then hybrid-bond it onto the finished CMOS periphery wafer, so the CMOS fab never touches the material.
why: Breaks the fab-acceptance barrier that kills new cells (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability): new memory layers in a $200-500M line instead of a $15B fab.

title: TSV-free HBM: ThruChip inductive links plus power-only vias
idea: HMC's power-hungry SerDes and Keio's ThruChip inductive-coupling interface both stalled, and HBM won while paying a large TSV tax. Stack DRAM dies with on-die spiral coils carrying data over near-field links (~0.1 pJ/bit). Keep only a sparse ring of large power TSVs at the die edge, so about 90% of TSVs and their keep-out zones disappear.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax (fact 6: 3x wafer area per bit, 20-30% yield loss). Targets ~1.5x area per bit and recovers most of the yield loss.

title: Irvine Sensors edge-stack revived: printed sidewall buses instead of TSVs
idea: Irvine Sensors' 1990s 'loaf-of-bread' cubes routed signals to die edges and metallized the stack's side, but died on thinning yield and coarse wiring. Route each DRAM die's I/O to edge pads, stack the dies, polish the side, and laser-direct-write or aerosol-print fine-pitch copper buses down the sidewall. No TSV pierces the array.
why: Removes the TSV area and yield tax (fact 6). Edge buses at 10 um pitch carry wide I/O. Claims ~2x bits per wafer area vs HBM.

title: Wide I/O fixed: thermal-break bond layer under DRAM-on-SoC
idea: JEDEC Wide I/O (DRAM stacked on mobile SoCs) died because SoC hot spots doubled DRAM refresh and because nobody wanted the TSV yield liability. Insert a porous low-k bonding layer with copper pillars that cuts heat flow into the DRAM about 5x. Add refresh zoning driven by a live SoC thermal map, so only rows above hot cores refresh fast.
why: Brings back 3D DRAM-on-logic for data-movement energy (fact 5: from 10-20 pJ/bit to under 1 pJ/bit) while capping refresh overhead (fact 3).

title: IBM racetrack made buildable: horizontal tracks from blanket stacked films
idea: IBM's racetrack memory died because its vertical U-shaped nanowires could not be built and domain walls pinned at etched edges. Deposit magnetic multilayer tracks as blanket films in a 3D-NAND-like layer stack, cut them with one vertical slit etch so each tier becomes a horizontal track, and put write and MTJ read heads on a vertical pillar. Short 16-domain tracks keep shifts under ~20 ns.
why: Density without a transistor per bit (fact 4), with mask count independent of tier count (fact 2). Targets ~16 bits per pillar per tier.

title: Toshiba chain-FeRAM revived as vertical chains of antiferroelectric cells
idea: Toshiba's chain-FeRAM (each cell a transistor in parallel with a ferroelectric capacitor, cells in series like NAND) died with PZT's hydrogen damage and a 2D footprint. Build it vertically: a pillar of gate-all-around tiers, each shunting a thin antiferroelectric ZrO2 capacitor ring, with one contact per chain. To read a tier, its shunt turns off while the others stay on.
why: One bitline contact per 16-32 tiers removes the 3D staircase/contact blocker (fact 2). AFE ZrO2 switches fast with high endurance and contains no lead.

title: ZettaCore's molecular redox storage repurposed as a charge-multiplying capacitor coating
idea: ZettaCore stored charge in porphyrin redox molecules on silicon but died on the 400C BEOL thermal budget. Graft thermally stable inorganic redox clusters (polyoxometalates) inside each 3D DRAM capacitor. Each cluster stores several electrons at a fixed potential, adding pseudocapacitance on top of the dielectric's.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 5-10x charge per um2 lets 3D tiers use short, low-AR capacitors (fact 2).

title: BeSang monolithic 3D fixed with seeded rapid-melt-growth tiers
idea: BeSang and other monolithic-3D ventures failed because low-temperature upper tiers had poor polysilicon transistors. Open seed windows to the single-crystal tier below and deposit amorphous Si over the oxide. Melt it with nanosecond laser pulses so it regrows laterally as single crystal from each seed (rapid-melt growth), while lower tiers stay under 450C.
why: Gives crystalline access transistors in every tier of 26+ tier 3D DRAM (fact 2) without a wafer bond per tier. Leakage approaches bulk Si (fact 3).

title: IBM Josephson lesson: run DRAM at 77 K, not superconducting
idea: IBM's 1980s Josephson computer program died largely for lack of a dense cryogenic memory. Instead of superconducting memory, run 3D DRAM tiers at liquid-nitrogen temperature. Access-transistor leakage drops by orders of magnitude, so retention stretches to hours, and the capacitor can shrink about 10x.
why: Removes refresh (fact 3) and the charge wall (fact 1), allowing short, cheap capacitors in many tiers. LN2 cooling avoids helium.

title: Rambus micro-threading revived as tier-granular activation in 3D DRAM
idea: Rambus micro-threading (rows split into small, independently activated pieces) was never adopted in planar DRAM because of decoder area and pin cost. In 3D DRAM, give each tier its own local wordline driver, so an activate opens one tier of one mat (~1 Kb) instead of an 8 Kb page.
why: Cuts the 128x overfetch and ~5.9 pJ per useful bit of random reads (fact 8) by ~8x, and shrinks the row-hammer blast radius (fact 9).

title: Hitachi PLEDM revived: h-BN barrier write transistor stacked on read gate
idea: Hitachi's 1990s PLEDM gain cell stacked a vertical multi-tunnel-barrier write transistor on the read transistor's gate, but died on leakage variability in its Si/SiN barriers. Rebuild the stacked write device with atomically uniform h-BN tunnel barriers so the storage node (the read gate) leaks below 1 aA. The result is a two-transistor gain cell in a one-transistor footprint.
why: No capacitor (fact 1), non-destructive read (fact 8), and retention long enough to cut refresh ~100x (fact 3), at ~4F2.

title: Matrix Semiconductor's write-once 3D ROM as a weights tier
idea: Matrix Semiconductor's 8-deck antifuse crosspoint (2001) failed because nobody wanted write-once storage. LLM inference does: burn model weights into a stack of antifuse decks over the accelerator's periphery, read in tens of ns. The weights no longer occupy DRAM, which then holds only KV cache and activations.
why: Does DRAM's job with less DRAM: weights are ~50-80% of inference memory, written once at ~10x DRAM's bits per mm2, with no refresh.

title: Spansion MirrorBit idea for DRAM: one split pillar, two capacitors
idea: MirrorBit stored two bits at the two ends of one charge-trap cell and died with Spansion's NOR business. Split each vertical access pillar into two half-channels with independent front and back gates. Each half connects to its own capacitor, one stacked on top and one buried below, so one 4F2 footprint holds two bits.
why: Effective 2F2 per bit (fact 4) with no extra EUV layers, doubling density per litho step.

title: Core-memory coincident selection for 3D tier addressing without staircases
idea: Ferrite core memory died on hand-threading labor, but its coincident-current X-Y selection was elegant. Make each 3D DRAM access transistor dual-gated, one gate on a horizontal tier plane and one on a vertical pillar gate, so a cell turns on only when both are driven. N planes by M pillars then select any cell with N+M drivers instead of a staircase and decoder per tier.
why: Removes staircase contact area and periphery growth in 3D DRAM (facts 2, 7). Decoder count grows with the square root of cell count instead of linearly.

title: Sun proximity communication revived as solder-free, demountable DRAM stacks
idea: Sun's capacitive proximity communication died on alignment and Oracle's acquisition. Carry die-to-die signals on capacitive pads in a clamped DRAM stack, deliver power through spring pins, and align dies with etched V-groove-and-ball kinematic mounts. With no solder or underfill, a failed die is unclamped and swapped, and dies separate cleanly for reuse at end of life.
why: Ends the HBM yield tax (fact 6) because a bad die is replaced rather than the stack scrapped. Repairable and fully recyclable.

title: Bubble-memory bootloop map applied to 3D DRAM strings
idea: Magnetic bubble chips shipped with defective minor loops masked by an on-chip loop map, then died on speed. Give every 3D DRAM die a rewritable defect map at the vertical-string level. Firmware retires defective or worn strings in the field, and the map's health record grades the die for second-life reuse.
why: Tolerating ~5% bad strings brings yield of 26+ tier 3D DRAM (fact 2) to economic levels, extends service life, and makes regrading and reuse possible.

title: Trilogy wafer-scale fixed with bondable patch-tile repair sites
idea: Gene Amdahl's Trilogy failed because wafer-scale defects could not be fixed after the wafer was built. Lay out a wafer-scale DRAM slab with a grid of empty landing sites over each region. After test, or later in a service depot, a known-good DRAM tile is bonded over any dead region and the router remaps it.
why: Wafer-scale economics for packaging and I/O energy (facts 5, 6) without the yield risk. The slab stays repairable over a 10-year life.

title: Alien Technology's fluidic self-assembly for replaceable DRAM mat chiplets
idea: Alien Technology's fluidic self-assembly (FSA) of tiny dies into shaped wells failed commercially for RFID. Make DRAM as 0.5 mm 'mat chiplets' that self-assemble into receptor wells on a periphery wafer and attach with low-melt solder. Bad chiplets are melted out and replaced, and at end of life all chiplets are released in a hot bath for retest and reuse.
why: Tiny chiplets yield ~99% (fact 4 capital), the periphery wafer can use an older US node (fact 7), and repair and recycling work at the chiplet level.

title: HMC logic base die made detachable with liquid-metal microbumps
idea: HMC died partly because its logic base die tied the DRAM stack to one controller generation. Join the base die to the DRAM core stack with gallium-indium liquid-metal microbumps held in polymer cups. Warming slightly releases the joint, so a stack can move to a new base die (for example a new CXL/UCIe PHY) and a failed base die can be replaced.
why: DRAM core dies outlive 2-3 controller generations, about doubling the useful life of scarce bits, and repair needs no stack scrap (fact 6).

title: IBM thermal conduction module rework for serviceable HBM packages
idea: IBM's 1980s thermal conduction modules let individual chips on a ceramic substrate be reworked several times, using spring-loaded pistons for cooling, but lost on cost. Mount HBM stacks on a glass substrate with reworkable solder joints and a spring piston per stack instead of a bonded lid. A depot can then desolder and replace one failed stack without discarding the accelerator.
why: Turns an accelerator board worth tens of thousands of dollars from scrap into a repair (fact 6 yield), recovering the good stacks and the GPU.

title: Project Ara lesson: optically coupled hot-swap memory tiles
idea: Google's Project Ara modular phone failed partly because its electro-permanent-magnet connectors could not carry enough bandwidth reliably. Couple swappable DRAM tiles to the host through short free-space optical links (VCSEL and photodiode arrays through a glass window), held by a mechanical latch. Tiles hot-swap with no wear-prone electrical connector.
why: Dense bandwidth with no contacts to wear (fact 5), plus field-replaceable, recyclable memory capacity.

title: Socketed DRAM chips return as MEMS micro-spring die sockets
idea: Socketed DIP DRAM was abandoned because of contact reliability and size. Use lithographically defined MEMS micro-springs, as in probe cards, as a permanent fine-pitch die socket on the interposer. A lid holds the HBM stack down, and it can be lifted out, retested and replaced.
why: Fixes HBM's irreparability and yield scrap (fact 6). Good stacks and interposers are reused instead of scrapped with the assembly.

title: Canon ELTRAN porous-silicon donor wafers reused for 3D DRAM tiers
idea: Canon's ELTRAN layer transfer (epitaxy on porous Si, split at the porous layer) lost to Smart Cut. It suits bonded 3D DRAM tiers well: grow each tier epitaxially on porous Si, bond, split, re-porosify the donor and repeat about 20 times.
why: Cuts crystal growth per tier ~20x, and with it demand for Spruce Pine quartz crucibles (a resource chokepoint), making many-tier bonded 3D DRAM affordable (fact 2). Donor wafers are recycled by design.

title: Optane write-off lesson: universal second-life interface on every DRAM die
idea: Intel's Optane exit ended in a large inventory write-down, partly because the dies worked only with one CPU interface. Put a small standardized test-and-reuse port (JTAG-like self-test plus a slow generic protocol) and a wear log on every DRAM die. Dies harvested from retired HBM and DDR modules can then be retested and repackaged into CXL capacity modules.
why: Adds usable supply from retired dies, perhaps 10-20% more bits per year at today's server refresh rates, without new fabs (capital intensity, scarcity).

title: Failed SrTiO3 DRAM capacitors revived with self-clearing electrodes
idea: SrTiO3 (k ~100+) DRAM capacitors were researched and abandoned because weak spots leaked and broke down. Use an ultra-thin top electrode that vaporizes locally around a breakdown site, as in self-healing metallized-film capacitors. Each defect is isolated, so the capacitor loses a tiny area instead of shorting.
why: Delivers the k ~70+ the charge wall calls for (fact 1), allowing lower-AR pillars (AR ~40) while preserving yield. Self-repair is built in.

title: Macronix self-healing flash applied: wordline-heater anneal of DRAM leakage tails
idea: Macronix showed around 2012 that flash cells heal when current through the wordline heats them for milliseconds, but never productized it. In 3D DRAM, pulse current through the metal wordlines during scheduled maintenance to heat cells locally to ~350-400C for microseconds. This anneals the trap sites behind the leakage tail and variable retention time.
why: Shrinks the <=13 fA leakage tail that sets refresh (fact 3), for ~2-4x longer refresh intervals over life. Repair happens in the field.

title: BCB polymer bonding repurposed as debond-on-demand tier interlayer
idea: BCB adhesive wafer bonding was abandoned for 3D stacking because it degrades above ~350C. Make that a feature: bond DRAM tiers with a thin, thermally decomposable polymer pierced by short copper nails for signals. At end of life a bake separates the tiers for retest and reuse, or for clean copper and silicon recovery.
why: Makes multi-tier stacks (facts 2, 6) recyclable into reusable dies or clean material streams instead of mixed shredder waste.

title: Rambus royalty lesson: open, interchangeable core-die standard for repairable stacks
idea: Rambus's royalty model and HMC's closed spec both slowed adoption. Define an open, royalty-free mechanical and electrical standard for the DRAM core dies inside a stack, so any vendor's die can replace a failed one. US government and hyperscaler buyers then require serviceable stacks built to this standard.
why: Turns stacks into repairable assemblies with multi-vendor supply, letting small US fabs sell core dies (U.S. manufacturability) and raising uptime per scarce bit.

title: HP's The Machine fixed: pooled memory racks with a refurbishment loop
idea: HPE's The Machine died betting on an unready memristor. Build the same memory-centric fabric with today's DRAM in CXL-attached pooled racks, sold as a service. Modules are hot-swapped, tested, refurbished and redeployed to lower tiers instead of retiring with the server.
why: Pooling cuts stranded DRAM (often 20-40% unused per server), and refurbishment roughly doubles module life, raising usable supply without new fabs.

title: Abandoned molybdenum gates revived as recoverable, US-sourced wordline metal
idea: Molybdenum gates were tried in early MOS and dropped for polysilicon because of oxidation and processing problems. Replace tungsten in buried and 3D wordlines with ALD Mo under a nitride cap that blocks oxidation, and design the stack so the Mo can be selectively leached and recovered at end of life.
why: Removes the tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) using U.S.-mined Mo, with lower resistivity at thin dimensions and closed-loop metal recovery.

title: ReRAM endurance failure fixed: strippable, re-coatable consumable memory layer
idea: ReRAM and PCM never replaced DRAM partly because the switching film wears out. Put the switching film as the top BEOL layer over a permanent CMOS base die, designed so a depot can plasma-strip and redeposit it. A worn die is then remanufactured instead of scrapped.
why: Lets cheap BEOL memories do DRAM's job despite finite endurance, while the expensive CMOS base (periphery, fact 7) is reused 3-5 times.

title: NEMS relay logic failure repurposed: relays isolate dead tiers
idea: Nano-electro-mechanical (NEMS) relay logic has not been adopted because contacts stick after billions of cycles. A spare-tier switch needs only a few dozen actuations, so put NEMS relays on each tier's power and signal rails. A shorted or leaky tier is physically disconnected, with zero leakage, and a spare tier switched in.
why: Keeps one bad tier from killing a 26+ tier 3D DRAM stack (fact 2 yield) or an HBM stack (fact 6), with repair in the field.

title: Staktek package stacking reborn as blade-stacked, edge-contact DRAM dies
idea: Staktek's stacked packages lost to TSVs because their flex leads were coarse. Mount each thinned DRAM die on a thin carrier blade with fine edge contacts, and slide the blades into a compression-contact backplane next to the processor. Any blade can be pulled and replaced.
why: Replaces TSVs (fact 6) with edge contacts and makes each die serviceable and recyclable, at density near HBM with no TSV yield loss.

title: Indium-free zinc-tin-oxide tiers revived for recyclable 3D DRAM
idea: Zinc tin oxide (ZTO) transistors lost to IGZO on mobility and etch control. 3D DRAM access devices need low leakage more than mobility, so use ZTO channels for the stacked tiers, with an all-oxide stack chosen so zinc and tin are recovered by a simple acid leach.
why: Avoids indium (China-dominated, scarce) in oxide-channel 3D DRAM (facts 2, 3), with a recycling route designed in.

title: HP hot-plug RAID memory revived as a parity tier in 3D stacks
idea: HP's hot-plug RAID memory was dropped because it gave up 20-25% of capacity to redundancy. Inside a 3D DRAM or HBM stack, add one XOR parity tier per 16 data tiers plus a spare. When a tier fails, its data is rebuilt onto the spare in the background and the stack stays in service.
why: About 6% overhead to survive a whole-tier failure, raising 3D stack yield and life (facts 2, 6) with repair built in.

title: AIST Minimal Fab repurposed as regional memory repair depots
idea: Japan's Minimal Fab (half-inch wafers in desk-sized tools) failed as production because its throughput was low. Repair does not need throughput: equip US regional depots with minimal-fab-style tools to rework stacks, rebond patch tiles, replace dies and re-ball modules.
why: Makes repairable designs economically real and builds US memory manufacturing jobs and capability at low capital (~$10-50M per depot).

title: Directed self-assembly patterning made viable by defect-tolerant repairable arrays
idea: Directed self-assembly (DSA) of block copolymers was dropped from DRAM roadmaps because its defect rates were too high. Use DSA to pattern 4F2 pillar arrays without EUV, and tolerate defect densities around 1e-4 through string sparing and defect maps updated in the field.
why: Cuts perhaps 2-3 of the 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4; depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost), with repairability absorbing DSA's defect rate.
